claims.text: Superconducting transition temperature in uncharacterized high-entropy alloys is primarily governed by the interplay of average valence electron count and lattice strain caused by atomic-size mismatch.
Average valence electron count and induced lattice strain modulate the electron–phonon coupling needed for Cooper-pair formation.
The proposed starting material is a uniformly mixed, single-phase solid solution containing at least five elements at no less than 5 atomic percent each.
Adding a sixth element can controllably increase or decrease the alloy's average valence electron count.
Adding the sixth element can modify lattice strain while preserving a homogeneous single-phase state.
The comparison series should be processed identically and measured below approximately 20 K.
Atomic-size differences produce local lattice distortions.
The compositional intervention produces shifts in the electronic density of states.
Changing average electron count tunes the density of states at the Fermi level.
Lattice distortions affect the phonon spectrum.
The combined electronic and phononic changes can optimize electron–phonon coupling.
An optimized balance of electron count and moderate lattice strain will increase Tc relative to the baseline alloy.
Departures from the proposed optimum will reduce Tc or suppress superconductivity.
The proposed mechanism applies only while the alloy remains a stable, single-phase random solid solution.
Phase separation or significant clustering caused by excessive strain can make the proposed mechanism inapplicable.
The quantitative relationship among electron count, lattice strain, and Tc is not established.
Failure of Tc to correlate significantly with the intended electron-count and strain changes in compositionally and structurally homogeneous samples would falsify the hypothesis.
Formation of secondary phases after addition of the sixth element would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: Phase separation or secondary-phase formation is defined as outside the hypothesis's applicability domain, but is also listed as an outcome that would falsify the hypothesis. A boundary violation that obscures the proposed mechanism is not by itself a decisive test of that mechanism.
